uni_note: These are widely recognised institutions, listed to help you start a shortlist. This is not a ranking: league tables change every year and suit different goals, so check each university's course, fees, entry rules and outcomes for your own subject.

usa.intro: The United States has the largest number of universities in the world and a flexible system: undergraduates can explore subjects before choosing a major, and many graduate students get paid assistantships. Applications are holistic, which means universities read your marks, essays, recommendations and activities together, not just one test score.

timeline.title: Explore and set a budget
timeline.text: Decide what you want to study, how much your family can spend per year, and whether you need aid. List 10 to 15 universities across three groups: ambitious, realistic and safe.

timeline.title: Plan tests
timeline.text: Undergraduate: SAT or ACT where required or recommended, plus TOEFL, IELTS or Duolingo. Graduate: GRE or GMAT where the programme asks for it. Book test dates early so you can retake if needed.

timeline.title: Build documents
timeline.text: Request transcripts, ask two or three teachers or managers for recommendation letters, and begin your personal statement or statement of purpose. Keep a list of activities, projects and achievements.

timeline.title: Write and polish essays
timeline.text: Write about your own story, not a copy of a sample. Ask a teacher to read for clarity. Many undergraduate applications go through the Common App; graduate applications go directly to each university's portal.

timeline.title: Submit applications
timeline.text: Early Action or Early Decision deadlines for undergraduates are usually in autumn; regular deadlines are in winter. Many graduate deadlines fall between December and January for the autumn intake. Pay the application fees and send official test scores.

timeline.title: Interviews, offers and aid
timeline.text: Some universities hold interviews. Compare offers and financial aid letters. Accept one offer by the stated deadline and pay the deposit.

timeline.title: Get the I-20 and apply for the F-1 visa
timeline.text: The university sends an I-20 after you show financial proof. Pay the SEVIS fee, fill the DS-160 form, book the visa interview and prepare to explain your study plan and funding clearly.

timeline.title: Prepare to travel
timeline.text: Arrange housing, health insurance, forex and flights. Join the university's international-student orientation groups so you meet people before you land.

costs.note: Private universities and out-of-state public universities are at the high end.
Many MS and PhD students receive assistantships that reduce or cover tuition.
Depends on city, dorm or shared apartment.
Cooking at home is cheaper than meal plans or eating out.
Most universities require it; many sell a student plan.
Cities with good public transport cost less.

costs.range: A few hundred US dollars in total
costs.note: Includes the visa fee and the SEVIS fee; check the current amounts on the official site.

psw.summary: The US system is called OPT (Optional Practical Training). You can work in your field of study for a limited time after you graduate. Some students also get CPT, which allows work as part of the course.
rules: OPT gives up to 12 months of work permission after you finish your degree. You apply for an employment authorisation document (EAD) in a set window around graduation.
If your degree is on the official STEM list, you can apply for a 24-month STEM OPT extension. That makes up to 36 months in total for eligible students.
For STEM OPT, your employer must be registered with E-Verify and you and your employer complete a training plan (Form I-983).
There is a limit on the number of days you can be unemployed during OPT. Keep track of it.
Longer-term work usually needs an employer to sponsor you, for example through the H-1B visa, which is selected by lottery and has annual limits.

scholarships.name: Fulbright-Nehru fellowships
scholarships.text: Funded by the US and Indian governments and run by USIEF. It is highly competitive and usually needs strong academics and a clear plan for how you will use your study.

scholarships.name: Graduate assistantships
scholarships.text: Universities hire graduate students as teaching or research assistants and pay a stipend, often along with a tuition waiver. You apply through the department.

scholarships.name: University merit and need-based aid
scholarships.text: Many universities give scholarships based on academics or financial need. Check each university's financial-aid page for international students.

scholarships.name: Tata Scholarship at Cornell
scholarships.text: Need-based support for eligible Indian undergraduates at Cornell University; check the Cornell page for current terms.

scholarships.name: JN Tata Endowment
scholarships.text: A loan scholarship for Indian students going abroad for higher studies; it has its own application cycle and eligibility.

scholarships.name: Inlaks Shivdasani Scholarships
scholarships.text: A private foundation scholarship for outstanding Indian students at leading universities abroad.

scholarships.name: Knight-Hennessy Scholars
scholarships.text: A leadership programme that funds graduate study at Stanford; applicants are selected from many countries.

faqs.q: Do I need the SAT to study in the USA?
faqs.a: Many universities are test-optional, but some require SAT or ACT scores. Check each university's policy for your intake year.

faqs.q: Can I work while studying in the USA?
faqs.a: F-1 students can usually work on campus up to a weekly limit during term. Off-campus work needs separate authorisation such as CPT or OPT.

faqs.q: How early should I apply?
faqs.a: Start 12 to 18 months before your intended start date. Autumn is the main intake.

uk.intro: The UK is popular because degrees are shorter: a bachelor's is usually three years and a master's often one year. That lowers total cost and gets you into work sooner. Undergraduate applications go through UCAS, and universities look closely at your subject marks and personal statement.

timeline.title: Choose course and universities
timeline.text: In the UK you apply for a specific course, not a general degree. Pick one subject and shortlist up to five universities for UCAS.

timeline.title: Check entry requirements
timeline.text: Look at the required Class 12 marks and subjects. Some courses ask for specific subjects or an admissions test, such as for medicine or Oxford and Cambridge.

timeline.title: Take English tests
timeline.text: IELTS Academic is the most common. If you need a visa, check whether the university needs a test approved for UK visas.

timeline.title: Write the personal statement
timeline.text: Explain why you want the course and show proof of interest: projects, reading, competitions and work experience. Ask a teacher for a reference.

timeline.title: Apply through UCAS or directly
timeline.text: UCAS deadlines for Oxford, Cambridge and medicine come earlier than for other courses. Most master's applications go directly to the university.

timeline.title: Receive offers and accept
timeline.text: Offers can be conditional on exam results or unconditional. Choose a firm choice and an insurance choice in UCAS, or accept directly.

timeline.title: Get the CAS and apply for the Student visa
timeline.text: The university issues a Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS). Apply online, pay the visa fee and the Immigration Health Surcharge, and give biometrics.

timeline.title: Plan housing and travel
timeline.text: Apply for university accommodation early because it fills fast. Arrange insurance, forex and travel.

costs.note: Medicine and some lab subjects cost more.
Most master's degrees last one year.
London is at the high end.
Supermarket cooking is cheaper than eating out.

costs.range: Charged per year of visa; about GBP 776 per year at the last update
costs.note: This gives access to the NHS; check the current rate on gov.uk.
Student railcards and bus passes reduce costs.
UCAS fee plus the visa fee; check gov.uk for current amounts.

psw.summary: The UK Graduate Route lets you stay and work, or look for work, after you complete a degree. You do not need an employer sponsor for this visa.
rules: The Graduate Route is currently 2 years after a bachelor's or master's degree and 3 years after a PhD.
You must apply from inside the UK, while your Student visa is still valid, and after your university has told the Home Office you completed the course.
The UK government has announced plans to shorten the Graduate Route for new applications in the coming years, so check gov.uk for the exact rule for your intake.
Longer-term work usually moves to a Skilled Worker visa, which needs a job from a licensed sponsor and a minimum salary or skill level.
While studying, Student visa holders can normally work part-time up to a weekly limit set in their visa conditions.

scholarships.name: Chevening Scholarships
scholarships.text: Funded by the UK government for future leaders. You usually need at least two years of work experience and a plan to return to your home country after the award.

scholarships.name: Commonwealth Scholarships
scholarships.text: For students from eligible Commonwealth countries who could not otherwise afford to study in the UK; see the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission for categories.

scholarships.name: GREAT Scholarships
scholarships.text: Part-funded awards from the British Council and UK universities for students from selected countries, including India.

scholarships.name: Rhodes Scholarship
scholarships.text: A prestigious scholarship that funds study at the University of Oxford; check the India constituency rules.

scholarships.name: Gates Cambridge Scholarship
scholarships.text: Funds students from outside the UK for full-time study at Cambridge, including India.

scholarships.name: Felix Scholarships
scholarships.text: For high-achieving Indian students at selected UK universities such as Oxford, SOAS and Reading.

scholarships.name: University merit awards
scholarships.text: Many universities give fee reductions or awards to international students based on grades; look on each university's funding page.

faqs.q: Can I work after studying in the UK?
faqs.a: Yes. The Graduate Route currently lets you stay for 2 years (3 for PhD) without a sponsor, and you can also move to a Skilled Worker visa if an employer sponsors you.

faqs.q: Is IELTS required?
faqs.a: Most universities need an English test. For the visa, some universities can assess your English themselves, so ask the university which test they need.

faqs.q: How many UCAS choices can I make?
faqs.a: You can choose up to five courses on a UCAS application.

germany.intro: Germany is the best-known destination for low-cost education because most public universities charge no tuition, including for international students. You still need to cover living costs, insurance and a blocked-account deposit, and you may need German for many programmes. Strong engineering and applied sciences make it a popular choice.

timeline.title: Check eligibility
timeline.text: Check how your Indian degree or Class 12 is recognised through the anabin database or the university's admissions page. Some students need a foundation course (Studienkolleg) or a year of Indian university first.

timeline.title: Pick language and programme
timeline.text: Choose an English-taught or German-taught programme. For German programmes, start learning German early (B2 or C1 is common).

timeline.title: Take APS certification
timeline.text: Indian applicants need an APS (Akademische Prüfstelle) certificate, which verifies your documents. Book it early because it can take weeks.

timeline.title: Take English tests
timeline.text: IELTS or TOEFL for English-taught courses. Some programmes also ask for GRE, GMAT or a portfolio.

timeline.title: Apply through uni-assist or the university
timeline.text: Many universities use uni-assist for international applications; others have their own portal. Winter semester deadlines are usually in mid-year (check each university).

timeline.title: Open a blocked account and get insurance
timeline.text: Deposit the required amount, roughly EUR 11,000 to 12,000, and arrange German health insurance. This is needed for the visa.

timeline.title: Apply for the national visa
timeline.text: Book an appointment at the German mission, submit the documents and wait for the decision. Processing can take weeks.

timeline.title: Register and get the residence permit
timeline.text: Register your address, enrol at the university and apply for the residence permit at the local immigration office.

costs.note: Baden-Wurttemberg charges non-EU students tuition, and some master's programmes and private universities charge fees.
Often includes a public-transport ticket.
Student dorms are cheaper but limited; big cities cost more.
University canteens (Mensa) are cheap.
Public student insurance is common.

costs.range: Roughly EUR 11,000 to 12,000 deposit per year
costs.note: You can withdraw a fixed monthly amount; check the current figure.

costs.range: Around EUR 75 for the national visa
costs.note: Check the German mission for the current fee.

psw.summary: After your degree you can apply for an 18-month residence permit to look for a job that matches your qualification.
rules: The job-seeker permit lasts up to 18 months after graduation. You can work during this period while searching.
Once you find a qualified job you can switch to a work permit or the EU Blue Card, which has a minimum salary threshold.
Blue Card holders can often apply for permanent residence after a few years of work; German skills can shorten the time.
During study, non-EU students can usually work 140 full days or 280 half days per year, plus student-assistant jobs at the university.
Learning German greatly improves your job prospects outside English-speaking companies.

scholarships.name: DAAD scholarships
scholarships.text: The German Academic Exchange Service funds many programmes. Search the DAAD scholarship database and check each programme's rules.

scholarships.name: DAAD WISE
scholarships.text: A programme that helps Indian students do summer research internships in science and engineering in Germany.

scholarships.name: Deutschlandstipendium
scholarships.text: A merit scholarship given by German universities and private sponsors; apply at your university once enrolled.

scholarships.name: Erasmus+
scholarships.text: European Union funding for student exchange and joint master's programmes involving German universities.

scholarships.name: Political foundation scholarships
scholarships.text: Foundations such as Konrad Adenauer and Friedrich Ebert offer awards, often with a focus on social engagement and academic merit.

faqs.q: Do I need to know German?
faqs.a: Not for English-taught programmes, but German helps with daily life and jobs. German-taught programmes need a language certificate.

faqs.q: Is it really free?
faqs.a: Most public universities do not charge tuition, but you pay a semester contribution and your living costs.

faqs.q: What is the APS certificate?
faqs.a: It is a document-verification certificate Indian students need before applying to German universities.

canada.intro: Canada offers a wide choice of universities and colleges, with programmes that often include co-op work terms. Rules for study permits and post-graduation work permits have been changing, so check the programme and the institution carefully before you apply.

timeline.title: Choose programme and province
timeline.text: Pick the programme first, then the province. Colleges teach practical diplomas; universities offer degrees. Check whether the institution is a designated learning institution (DLI).

timeline.title: Check post-study work eligibility
timeline.text: Not every programme or institution qualifies for a post-graduation work permit. Check the current list and the field-of-study rules before you pay.

timeline.title: Take English tests
timeline.text: IELTS Academic or TOEFL are common. Some institutions accept Duolingo; confirm what the institution accepts for admission and for the study permit.

timeline.title: Prepare documents
timeline.text: Gather transcripts, a statement of purpose, references and proof of funds. Graduate programmes may ask for a professor's support or a research proposal.

timeline.title: Apply to institutions
timeline.text: Deadlines vary: many fall in winter for the September intake, and colleges often have January and May intakes as well.

timeline.title: Pay deposit and get the acceptance letter
timeline.text: Accept your offer and pay the deposit to receive the Letter of Acceptance. In some provinces you also need a provincial attestation letter.

timeline.title: Apply for the study permit
timeline.text: Apply online with your acceptance letter, proof of funds, identity documents and a clear study plan. Give biometrics and a medical exam if asked.

timeline.title: Plan arrival
timeline.text: Book housing for the first month, arrange insurance and carry key documents. Learn about health coverage in your province.

costs.note: Colleges are usually cheaper than universities.
Research master's may be funded.
Toronto and Vancouver are more expensive.
Grocery prices have risen; plan carefully.
Depends on the province; some provide coverage after a waiting period.
Student transit passes are usually discounted.

costs.range: About CAD 150 plus a biometrics fee at the last update
costs.note: Check IRCC for the current fees.

psw.summary: The Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) lets graduates of eligible programmes work in Canada after studying.
rules: The PGWP length usually matches the length of your programme, up to a maximum of 3 years.
Your institution and programme must be eligible, and recent rules add language and field-of-study conditions for some graduates; check IRCC before you apply.
During study, students can usually work off campus up to a weekly limit; the cap has changed recently, so verify the current figure.
Canadian work experience can help you qualify for permanent residence through Express Entry or provincial programmes, but there is no guarantee.
Apply for the PGWP within the time window after you receive your final marks and while your permit is valid.

scholarships.name: Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarships
scholarships.text: A national scholarship for doctoral students, nominated by the university; apply through your chosen Canadian institution.

scholarships.name: Lester B. Pearson International Scholarship
scholarships.level: Undergraduate at the University of Toronto
scholarships.text: A full-support scholarship for outstanding international students; the school nominates candidates.

scholarships.name: UBC International Leader of Tomorrow Award
scholarships.text: Need-based awards for international students at the University of British Columbia.

scholarships.name: Mitacs Globalink Research Internship
scholarships.text: Summer research internships in Canada for students from selected countries including India.

scholarships.name: Shastri Indo-Canadian Institute fellowships
scholarships.text: Fellowships that support academic exchange between India and Canada.

scholarships.name: Entrance awards at universities
scholarships.text: Many Canadian universities award entrance scholarships automatically based on grades; check each institution's page.

faqs.q: Is Canada easier than other countries?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Study-permit and work-permit rules change often, so check IRCC and your province before you apply.

faqs.q: Colleges or universities?
faqs.a: Universities award degrees; colleges offer diplomas and applied programmes. Both can lead to a work permit, subject to the rules for that programme.

faqs.q: Do I need the GRE?
faqs.a: Only some graduate programmes ask for it; check the programme page.

australia.intro: Australia is known for high-quality universities, a strong support system for international students and a wide range of courses, from engineering to nursing. Student-visa rules have been tightened in recent years, so a clear study plan and genuine-student statement are important.

timeline.title: Pick a course and intake
timeline.text: Australia has two main intakes: February and July. Choose the course, the university and a study plan that you can explain clearly in your visa application.

timeline.title: Check requirements
timeline.text: Look at the academic entry marks, English requirement and any prerequisites. Some courses need a portfolio or interview.

timeline.title: Take English tests
timeline.text: IELTS, TOEFL, PTE or Duolingo are accepted at many universities. Confirm which tests the university and the visa accept.

timeline.title: Apply to the university
timeline.text: Applications go to the university or its approved agent. Upload transcripts, English results, ID and a statement of purpose.

timeline.title: Accept and pay the deposit
timeline.text: Accept the offer and pay the tuition deposit. You then receive a Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE).

timeline.title: Arrange OSHC
timeline.text: Overseas Student Health Cover is compulsory for the visa. Buy it for the whole duration of your visa.

timeline.title: Apply for the student visa
timeline.text: Apply for subclass 500 online, with funds, genuine-student statement, health checks and biometrics as required.

timeline.title: Plan housing and arrival
timeline.text: Book short-term accommodation and learn about the pickup service. Open a local bank account after arrival.

costs.note: Medicine and veterinary courses cost more.
Coursework master's are usually one and a half to two years.
Sydney and Melbourne cost the most.
Cooking at home is cheaper.

costs.range: A few hundred to around a thousand AUD per year
costs.note: Compare approved providers.
Student concession cards help.

costs.range: Above AUD 1,500 at the last update
costs.note: The fee has increased; check the Department of Home Affairs.

psw.summary: The Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) allows eligible graduates to stay and work for a limited time after study.
rules: The 485 visa length depends on the qualification, and it is usually 2 to 4 years; recent updates have changed some rules and age limits.
You must apply within a set period after finishing your course and meet English and health requirements.
Work rights during study are capped per fortnight in term time; check the current limit.
Studying in some regional areas can add extra time or give other benefits.
Skilled-work or employer-sponsored visas are the usual route to longer stays.

scholarships.name: Australia Awards
scholarships.text: Government-funded awards for students from selected countries; check whether your country and field are included.

scholarships.name: Destination Australia
scholarships.text: Support for students studying at regional campuses; check eligibility on the official site.

scholarships.name: Melbourne International Undergraduate Scholarship
scholarships.text: A merit-based award for international students at the University of Melbourne.

scholarships.name: Monash International Merit Scholarship
scholarships.text: A merit-based award given by Monash to eligible international students.

scholarships.name: UNSW and University of Sydney international scholarships
scholarships.text: These universities run their own international-student awards with different eligibility and deadlines.

scholarships.name: Research scholarships
scholarships.text: Universities offer research stipends and tuition support; contact potential supervisors early.

faqs.q: What is a genuine student statement?
faqs.a: A written explanation showing why you want to study in Australia, why this course and how it fits your career. It should be honest and specific.

faqs.q: Can I work in Australia while studying?
faqs.a: Yes, but there is a limit on hours per fortnight during term time. Check the Department of Home Affairs for the current limit.

faqs.q: Which tests are accepted?
faqs.a: Most universities accept IELTS, TOEFL and PTE; many accept Duolingo for admission. Confirm for your course.

ireland.intro: Ireland is an English-speaking EU country with strong technology, pharma and finance industries. It is smaller than other destinations, so universities are close-knit and cities are easy to move around. Accommodation can be expensive, especially in Dublin.

timeline.title: Pick institutions
timeline.text: Ireland has universities, technological universities and institutes. Shortlist courses and check eligibility for international applicants.

timeline.title: Check requirements
timeline.text: Look at the Class 12 marks needed and any subject conditions. Some courses need interviews or portfolios.

timeline.title: Take English tests
timeline.text: IELTS or TOEFL are the usual routes. Check each institution's requirement.

timeline.title: Apply directly
timeline.text: International applicants usually apply directly to the university or through its portal, not through the CAO. Upload documents and a statement of purpose.

timeline.title: Accept and pay the deposit
timeline.text: Accept the offer and pay the deposit to receive proof of payment, which is needed for the visa.

timeline.title: Apply for the study visa
timeline.text: Apply online with documents, proof of funds, insurance and academic records. Provide biometrics as instructed.

timeline.title: Find housing
timeline.text: Start looking early; in Dublin accommodation is limited. Apply for campus housing as soon as you accept the offer.

timeline.title: Register with immigration
timeline.text: Register with immigration services within the required time after you arrive to receive your permission to stay (Stamp 2).

costs.note: Medicine and some professional courses cost more.
Many master's last one year.
Dublin is the most expensive.
Supermarkets and student meal deals help.
Required for non-EU students.
Student Leap cards give discounts.

costs.range: A modest government fee at the last update
costs.note: Check the Irish immigration site for the current amount.

psw.summary: Ireland's stay-back scheme (Third Level Graduate Programme) lets graduates remain to look for work or take up employment.
rules: Bachelor's graduates can usually get up to 12 months and master's or PhD graduates up to 24 months, if they meet the scheme's conditions.
Your course must be on the approved list and you must have studied full-time at an eligible institution.
A Critical Skills Employment Permit is a common route to longer-term work if you get a job in an eligible occupation.
While studying, international students can generally work up to 20 hours per week in term time and 40 hours during holidays.
Always confirm the latest rules with Irish immigration services.

universities.name: Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland (RCSI)

scholarships.name: Government of Ireland International Education Scholarship
scholarships.text: A government scholarship for non-EU students, nominated by participating institutions.

scholarships.name: Trinity Global Excellence Scholarship
scholarships.text: Merit-based support for international students at Trinity College Dublin.

scholarships.name: UCD Global Excellence Scholarships
scholarships.text: Awards for strong international applicants at University College Dublin.

scholarships.name: Erasmus Mundus joint programmes
scholarships.text: EU-funded joint master's programmes that involve study in Ireland and other European countries.

scholarships.name: University-specific awards
scholarships.text: Several Irish universities offer fee reductions for international students; check each funding page.

faqs.q: Is Ireland cheaper than the UK?
faqs.a: Tuition is often slightly lower, but housing in Dublin can be costly. Compare total yearly costs.

faqs.q: Can I work after my degree?
faqs.a: Eligible graduates can use the stay-back scheme for 12 or 24 months depending on the qualification.

faqs.q: Do I apply through the CAO?
faqs.a: International students usually apply directly to the university, but check each institution.

singapore.intro: Singapore is a compact Asian hub with highly ranked universities, a strong link to industry and a short flight home. Competition for places is intense, and there is no automatic post-study work visa, so planning for internships and job offers matters.

timeline.title: Research institutions
timeline.text: Singapore has six autonomous universities plus polytechnics and private institutes. Choose based on the course, entry marks and cost.

timeline.title: Check admission rules
timeline.text: Indian applicants usually apply with Class 12 results and may need SAT or other tests at some universities. Check each university's page.

timeline.title: Take tests
timeline.text: IELTS or TOEFL for English proof; SAT, GRE or GMAT where required.

timeline.title: Apply to universities
timeline.text: Applications are online. Submit transcripts, essays and recommendations. Some courses involve interviews or portfolios.

timeline.title: Accept and consider tuition grants
timeline.text: Tuition grants reduce fees but require you to work in Singapore for a set period after graduation (a bond). Read the bond terms carefully.

timeline.title: Apply for the Student's Pass
timeline.text: The university usually submits the application on your behalf. You receive an In-Principle Approval letter.

timeline.title: Arrange housing and medical checks
timeline.text: Apply for hostel accommodation or look for rentals. Complete the required medical checks.

timeline.title: Collect your pass
timeline.text: Complete the formalities to receive your Student's Pass and register at the university.

costs.note: Tuition grants reduce fees but come with a work bond.
Professional programmes can be higher.
Hostels are cheaper; private rentals cost more.
Hawker centres are affordable.

costs.range: A few hundred SGD per year
costs.note: Medical insurance is part of the pass requirements.
Student concession passes help.

costs.range: A modest government fee at the last update
costs.note: Check ICA for the current amount.

psw.summary: Singapore does not have a dedicated post-study work visa. Most graduates need an employer to apply for a work pass.
rules: An Employment Pass is for professionals and has a minimum salary and a points system.
An S Pass is for mid-level skilled workers and has its own salary and quota rules.
Some graduates from approved institutions may be eligible for a limited-duration pass to look for a job, so check the Ministry of Manpower.
Part-time work during study is limited and depends on your institution and pass conditions.
Internships and early networking are important because job offers are what unlock a work pass.

universities.name: Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD)

scholarships.name: Singapore International Graduate Award (SINGA)
scholarships.text: A research scholarship for doctoral students in science and engineering offered through Singapore agencies and universities.

scholarships.name: A*STAR graduate scholarships
scholarships.text: Research scholarships from the Agency for Science, Technology and Research in Singapore.

scholarships.name: NUS and NTU research scholarships
scholarships.text: Stipend and tuition support for research students; apply through the university.

scholarships.name: MOE Tuition Grant
scholarships.text: A fee subsidy for eligible international students that requires a work bond with Singapore after graduation.

scholarships.name: University merit scholarships
scholarships.text: Universities give merit scholarships to strong applicants; check each university's financial aid page.

faqs.q: Is it easy to get into NUS or NTU?
faqs.a: No. Competition is high, so strong marks, subject depth and activities matter.

faqs.q: Can I stay after my degree?
faqs.a: Only with a work pass from an employer or another eligible pass. There is no automatic stay-back.

faqs.q: What is the tuition grant bond?
faqs.a: If you take a tuition grant, you agree to work in Singapore for a set period after you graduate.
